To bereave someone means to cause them to lose a loved one through death. It captures the act of being robbed — cruelly and permanently — of someone you deeply love.

Think of it this way: death doesn't just take a person away from the world. It takes them away from you specifically — from your life, your home, your daily routine. That painful, personal sense of being stripped of someone you love is exactly what "bereave" describes.
Why You Almost Never See It Used Directly

Here's something important: in modern English, "bereave" is almost never used as a straightforward action verb the way you'd say "She opened the door." You won't typically hear someone say "The accident bereaved him."

Instead, this word almost always appears in its passive form — meaning something happened to a person, rather than someone doing it. This makes perfect sense, because no one chooses to lose someone. It happens to you.

So in real life, you'll see it like this:

"She was bereaved of her husband last winter."
(= Death took her husband away from her.)
Its Two Past Participle Forms — and Why They Matter

This is where "bereave" gets really interesting. It has two different past participle forms, and they are used differently:

1. Bereaved

Used specifically and exclusively when the loss is caused by death.

"The bereaved family sat quietly in the front row."
"She is a bereaved mother."
"Support groups exist for the bereaved." (here, "the bereaved" is used as a noun, meaning people who have lost someone to death)

When you say someone is bereaved, you are telling the listener something very precise: this person has lost someone through death. Nothing else — not divorce, not a friend moving away, not a breakup — qualifies. Only death.

2. Bereft

This is the other past participle, and it works differently. While bereaved is tied strictly to death, bereft is used more broadly to describe being completely stripped of something — whether it's a person, a feeling, a quality, or an abstract thing.

"After the argument, he felt utterly bereft." (a deep, hollow sense of loss — not necessarily death)
"The speech was bereft of any substance." (completely lacking in substance)
"She stood there, bereft of words." (unable to find words)

So bereft carries the emotional feeling of bereave — that emptiness, that sense of being robbed — but it can apply to losing hope, joy, meaning, ideas, or anything that once gave your life richness.
The Emotional Weight of the Word

"Bereave" and its family of words are not neutral or casual. They carry enormous emotional gravity. When you use "bereaved," you are signaling:

  • The loss is permanent. There is no going back.
  • The loss is not chosen. It was imposed by death.
  • The grief is deep and legitimate.

This is why the word is used carefully and respectfully — in obituaries, grief counseling, condolence letters, and literature. It treats the mourning person's pain with full seriousness.
Quick Summary of the Word Family

FormMeaning / Use
  • Bereave — the base verb; to cause someone to lose a loved one through death
  • Bereaved — past participle/adjective; specifically describes grief due to death
  • Bereft — past participle/adjective; describes being stripped of something (broader use, not limited to death)
  • Bereavement — the noun form; the state of grief after losing someone to death
  • The bereaved — a noun phrase; refers to people who are grieving a death
Examples That Show the Full Picture

"The earthquake bereaved thousands of families."
(Death caused them to lose their loved ones.)

"He was bereaved of his only son."
(His son died, leaving him in grief.)

"The counselor offered support to the bereaved."
(Those who lost someone to death.)

"Without her, he felt completely bereft."
(A deep, hollow emptiness — not necessarily from death.)

"The town was bereft of hope after the factory closed."
(Entirely lacking in hope.)
If you had to remember just one thing: to bereave is to have death steal your loved one from you — and to be bereaved is to carry that loss. It is one of the most human words in the English language.
